destination.title: The Stop Was Illegal — the Supreme Court Kept the Evidence Anyway

short51: An officer stops a man for no reason.
He runs his name and hits an
old traffic warrant.
A search then finds a small amount of drugs.
If the stop was illegal can that
evidence be used against you?
There's a rule for this:
the exclusionary rule.
Evidence from an illegal search is normally thrown out.
And everyone agreed this stop was illegal.
Utah conceded there was no reasonable suspicion.
So why did the drugs stay in?
Because that old warrant found mid-stop might
break the chain to the evidence.
Courts call it attenuation weighed by time
intervening events and police flagrancy.
In twenty sixteen five to three the
Court said the evidence stays.
The stop was still illegal but the
warrant attenuated the chain.
In dissent Justice Sotomayor warned it treats
you as the subject of a carceral
state just waiting to be cataloged.
The stop was never legal.
A warrant just made it pay off.
Watch the full case on the channel.
Follow for more.

candidate_payload_lines: The stop is stated as ILLEGAL in HOOK/ACT_1/ACT_2 ("That stop was not legal", "the state of Utah admitted it", "the reasonable suspicion the law requires"); it is NEVER called legal.
Sotomayor "carceral state" passage and "anyone's dignity" line quoted VERBATIM and attributed to the dissent ("Speaking for the dissent", "still speaking in dissent").
Across the lot a detective has been watching that house on and off for about a week, because a caller he never met left an anonymous tip that people were dealing drugs inside.
And the Supreme Court of the United States said that was the right result, even though everyone agreed the stop that started it should never have happened.
The case is called Utah versus Strieff, decided in 2016.
In June of 2016, the Court gave its answer, and it sided with the state of Utah.
After 2016, the honest answer is that it can, so long as the search that turns it up is tied to something like a warrant rather than to the stop itself.
Sits near the top of the 2,120-2,140 band (cap 2,141) so the ~5-8% fast TTS still lands inside the ~12-min runtime.
Methamphetamine named once, clinically, never dwelt on; Strieff (living person, R2) shown by symbol only, not glorified.
era_note: SET THIS. Modern stock footage is only usable if the case is modern; a 1960s case dressed in present-day footage reads wrong.

shorts.angle: If you are one of the many Americans carrying a small outstanding warrant, an unlawful stop becomes almost free for the officer who makes it.
shorts.avoids: The existing Short explains attenuation and quotes the dissent inside the Utah case; this cut is the ordinary unpaid fine or missed court date that makes the rule reach you.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: Does anything in the ruling stop an officer from stopping people at random to go looking for that warrant?

lines.text: An unpaid fine sitting in a database can turn an unlawful police stop into a search that holds up in court.
source_lines: The illegal stop becomes almost free.

lines.text: A very large number of Americans have some kind of outstanding warrant. Very often for something small. An unpaid fine, a missed court date, an old traffic ticket.
source_lines: A very large number of Americans have some kind of outstanding warrant, very often for something small, an unpaid fine, a missed court date, an old traffic ticket.

lines.text: If you are one of them, an officer who stops you with no legal reason can run your name, find that warrant, arrest you, and search you.
source_lines: If you are one of them, an officer who stops you with no legal reason can run your name, find that warrant, arrest you, and search you, and under this rule most of what he finds will hold up.

lines.text: And under this rule most of what he finds will hold up. The illegal stop becomes almost free.
source_lines: and under this rule most of what he finds will hold up. The illegal stop becomes almost free.

lines.text: Normally that evidence disappears. When police search illegally, whatever they turn up is thrown out of the case.
source_lines: If the police search you illegally, the evidence they turn up is normally thrown out.
Lawyers call it the exclusionary rule, and the idea is simple.

lines.text: The rule has exceptions. One is attenuation, when the link is so thinned out the connection barely holds.
source_lines: But the rule has never been absolute.
The name for that idea is attenuation.
Attenuated just means thinned out, so far removed from the first mistake that the connection barely holds.

lines.text: The warrant in Utah versus Strieff existed before the stop. It was valid and outstanding, so the search rode on it, not the stop.
source_lines: That warrant existed before the detective ever stopped Strieff.
It was valid, it was outstanding, and it commanded the detective to make an arrest the moment it surfaced.
That search is legal on its own terms, because it rides on the warrant, not on the stop.

lines.text: The stop was still illegal. The Court never pretended otherwise. It just stopped mattering to whether the drugs came into court.
source_lines: The stop was still illegal. The Court never pretended otherwise.

shorts.angle: A second dissent in the same case went after arithmetic, arguing the ruling raises an officer's incentive to make a stop he has no right to make.

lines.text: There were two dissents in this case. The second one is about arithmetic, and almost nobody quotes it.
source_lines: Then came the dissents, and this is where the case became one of the most quoted of the decade.

lines.text: Before this ruling, an officer who made an illegal stop got nothing for it. That was the point.
source_lines: Before this ruling, an officer who made an illegal stop got nothing for it, and that was the point.

lines.text: Justice Elena Kagan wrote separately, going after the incentive the majority had just handed the police. Now, she warned, the math changes.
source_lines: Justice Elena Kagan wrote a second dissent, going after the incentive the majority had just handed the police.
Now, she warned, the math changes.

lines.text: The officer's incentive to violate the Constitution thus increases, she wrote in dissent. From here on, he sees potential advantage in stopping individuals without reasonable suspicion.
source_lines: The officer's incentive to violate the Constitution thus increases, she wrote.
From here on, he sees potential advantage in stopping individuals without reasonable suspicion

lines.text: The majority called the warrant a genuine intervening circumstance. It broke the chain, and the evidence from that search stayed in the case.
source_lines: That, the Court said, was a genuine intervening circumstance.
The warrant broke the chain. The evidence stays.

lines.text: The Court also judged the officer's conduct at most negligent, not flagrant, which tipped the third factor toward letting the evidence in.
source_lines: On the third factor, the majority found the detective's conduct was at most negligent, not flagrant.
The more flagrant the misconduct, the more the Court wants to punish it by throwing the evidence out.

lines.text: She called that exactly the temptation the exclusionary rule is supposed to remove, and the majority had just restored it.

lines.text: Her side lost. Three votes, not five. And of the two dissents, the one that did the math is the one nobody quotes.
